Its 7 May 2026 analysis by Ryan Nunn put AI's estimated effect on employment and real hourly wages in the average exposed occupation close to zero and statistically indistinguishable from it.
evidence.confounder: Falling CPS response rates and survey noise; AI-exposure measures are imperfect; the Budget Lab itself notes that weak payroll growth reflects lower net immigration, not only labor demand.

evidence.text: New York Fed researchers Richard Audoly, Miles Guerin and Giorgio Topa found in Lightcast job-posting data that postings for more AI-exposed occupations declined relative to others, but the divergence began before ChatGPT's release in late 2022, stabilized after 2023 and was not concentrated in entry-level exposed jobs (Liberty Street Economics, 14 May 2026). They concluded that postings give little indication of a distinct AI-driven decline in labor demand.
evidence.confounder: Postings measure intent, not hires, and the data are private (Lightcast); the overall hiring slowdown since 2022 tracks the rate cycle; the exposure measure is built from one AI developer's usage data.

evidence.text: The OECD's Economic Outlook of 3 June 2026 reported no signs of widespread labour displacement from business adoption of AI at the industry level: vacancies in the most AI-exposed industries rose more than in other sectors over the year to April 2026 in most economies with data. The United States was the notable exception to that vacancy pattern.
evidence.confounder: Industry-level measures are coarse and can miss shifts within industries; the US, the economy this tracker centres on, is the exception to the vacancy finding; the 2026 energy-price shock affects all sectors.

evidence.text: Census Bureau economists and co-authors, using the 2026 AI supplement to the Business Trends and Outlook Survey, found that 18% of US firms used AI in at least one function in November 2025 to January 2026 (32% employment-weighted), that 66% used it to augment tasks and that employment reductions were rare at 2% (NBER working paper 35141, April 2026). They also found that functional deployment of AI and operational investment in it were associated with employment declines.
evidence.confounder: Self-reported survey with low adoption so far (18% of firms), so small effects are expected at this stage; the association between deeper deployment and employment declines cuts the other way.

evidence.text: A University of Warwick working paper by Peter John Lambert and Yannick Schindler (May 2026), using 243 million new hires and 407 million job postings in the US, UK, Canada and Australia over 2017-2025, found that a two-standard-deviation increase in exposure to generative AI, or in exposure to work from home, each predicted a fall of about 5 percentage points in the junior share of new hires by 2025. Estimated together, the work-from-home effect remained while the AI coefficient shrank sharply and was often statistically indistinguishable from zero.
evidence.confounder: AI exposure and work-from-home exposure are highly correlated, so separating them depends on model choices; the Stanford ADP study reports its young-worker gap persists with remote-work controls; data end in 2025.

evidence.text: In a preprint not yet peer reviewed (5 January 2026), Morgan R. Frank and four co-authors report that, in monthly US unemployment insurance records, unemployment risk in AI-exposed occupations began rising in early 2022, months before ChatGPT's release. They also report from LinkedIn profiles that graduate cohorts from 2021 onward entered AI-exposed jobs at lower rates than earlier cohorts, with the gap opening before late 2022.
evidence.ratingNote: An arXiv preprint has neither peer review nor an institutional publisher, so we rate its findings as the named authors' own claims.
evidence.confounder: Preprint, not yet peer reviewed; the 2022 rate hikes and the tech-sector correction coincide with the early-2022 rise; an earlier trend does not rule out an AI effect added later.

evidence.text: Richmond Fed economists Katarína Borovičková and Claudia Macaluso estimated from CPS data that workers in less AI-exposed occupations account for roughly half of the decline in the aggregate unemployment outflow rate from July 2023 to March 2026, while strongly attached workers in highly exposed occupations, whose own job-finding rates fell the most, account for at most about one-third (Economic Brief 26-27, August 2026). They conclude that AI exposure is an important but not dominant factor, and they judge the AI-related structural component to be growing and without precedent except for the spread of personal computers in the early 2000s.
evidence.confounder: A flows decomposition is accounting, not causal identification; falling CPS response rates; the rate cycle affects all groups.

evidence.text: Richmond Fed economists Katarína Borovičková and Claudia Macaluso found in CPS data that job-finding rates of unemployed workers, which historically moved together over the business cycle across quartiles of AI exposure (measured with Michael Webb's patent-based index), have diverged since 2023, with the largest declines for workers from highly AI-exposed occupations (Economic Brief 26-26, August 2026).
evidence.confounder: Correlation, not causation; AI-exposed occupations cluster in tech and finance, which were hit by the 2022-23 rate rise and the post-pandemic tech correction; falling CPS response rates.

evidence.text: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen of Stanford found in ADP payroll data through June 2026 no evidence of widespread economy-wide job displacement, but employment of workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations stood 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, a gap that has widened since August 2025 (August 2026 update). They report that the estimates attenuate when controlling for education, show some divergent trends before generative AI and are larger than in national survey benchmarks.
evidence.confounder: Education and the post-pandemic shift to remote work; the ADP sample differs from national data, where the gap is smaller; some pre-trends before generative AI.

evidence.text: Dallas Fed economists Tyler Atkinson and Shane Yamco found in CPS microdata (12-month moving averages) that the employment share of workers aged 20-24 in the most AI-exposed occupations slipped from 16.4% in November 2022 to 15.5% in September 2025 while other age and exposure groups rose or held steady, mainly because fewer young people entered those jobs: the rate at which young labor-force entrants found work in the most-exposed occupations fell by more than 3 percentage points from its November 2023 peak, which they say is not a typical cyclical pattern (6 January 2026). They estimate that even if all of the employment decline became unemployment it would add only 0.1 percentage point to the aggregate rate since November 2022.
evidence.confounder: Education and other traits correlated with exposure (the authors' own caveat); small CPS cells for young workers; data end in September 2025.

evidence.text: St. Louis Fed researchers Serdar Ozkan and Nicholas Sullivan found a 0.47 correlation across occupations between AI exposure and the rise in unemployment rates from 2022 to 2025 in CPS data (0.57 using a measure of actual AI adoption), with computer and mathematical occupations among the steepest rises, and stated that the result is correlation, not causation (26 August 2025).
evidence.confounder: Correlation, not causation (the authors' caveat): post-pandemic monetary tightening, economic uncertainty and chance timing; exposure measures differ between studies.

evidence.text: The prime-age (25-54) employment-population ratio (fred:LNS12300060) was 80.7% in September 2026, above its January 2020 level of 80.6% and just below its 2023-24 high of 80.9%, while the unemployment rate (fred:UNRATE) was 4.2% in September 2026, down from 4.5% in November 2025 and inside its 2015-2019 range of 3.5% to 5.7%.
evidence.confounder: The business cycle, falling CPS response rates, and lower net immigration slowing labor-force growth; a stable aggregate can hide shifts within groups.

evidence.text: Nonfarm business output per hour (fred:OPHNFB) reached an index of 120.017 in the second quarter of 2026, which we calculate as annualized growth of 2.5% since the fourth quarter of 2022 and 2.2% over the year, with a quarterly annualized rate (fred:PRS85006092) of 1.4% in Q2 2026. That pace sits above the 1.5% a year of 2007Q4-2019Q4 and below the 3.1% a year of the 1995Q4-2004Q4 IT-era pickup.
evidence.confounder: The business cycle and revisions; AI capital spending itself lifts measured output; Fed Chair Warsh told Congress on 14 July 2026 that strong productivity growth predates gains from AI adoption.

evidence.text: The Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker's median hourly wage growth, as a 12-month moving average, was 3.9% in August 2026 for professional and management occupations against 3.5% for service occupations (fred:FRBATLWGT12MMUMHWGOSCPM, fred:FRBATLWGT12MMUMHWGOSCS), and 3.6% for finance and business services against 3.5% for leisure and hospitality (fred:FRBATLWGT12MMUMHWGIFBS, fred:FRBATLWGT12MMUMHWGILH). We calculate both gaps (0.4 and 0.1 percentage point) as inside their 2015-2019 ranges (-0.1 to 1.0 and -0.5 to 1.0); over the year professional and management slowed more than service occupations (0.7 against 0.4 point), while finance and business services slowed slightly less than leisure and hospitality (0.9 against 1.0 point).
evidence.confounder: Inflation and the business cycle, falling CPS response rates, and broad occupation and industry groups that mix exposed and unexposed jobs.

evidence.text: Information-sector employment (fred:USINFO) was 2,739,000 in September 2026, 12.1% below its November 2022 high in the series since 2015 and 4.2% lower than a year earlier, and the sector's hires rate (bls:JTS510000000000000HIR) fell to 1.6% in August 2026, below its 2017-2019 range of 2.4% to 3.5%, matching its October 2023 low and above only April 2020's 1.5%.
evidence.confounder: The correction from pandemic-era tech over-hiring and the 2022-23 rate rise; secular decline in publishing and broadcasting within the sector; one month of JOLTS industry data is noisy and revised.

evidence.text: Compensation of employees (fred:COE) was 49.9% of gross domestic income (fred:GDI) in the second quarter of 2026 by our calculation, the lowest in the series files since 2015 and down from 51.2% in late 2024, while after-tax corporate profits (fred:CPATAX) rose to 11.8% of GDI, the highest in that span. Both shares had already left their 2015-2019 ranges (52.5% to 53.5% and 9.2% to 10.2%) before ChatGPT's release, the profit share in 2021 and the compensation share in early 2022, and held near 51.2-51.5% and 10.3-10.9% from mid-2022 through 2024 before moving further in 2025-26.
evidence.confounder: Labor's share stepped down in 2022, before generative AI spread; 2026 inflation and the energy-price shock lift nominal profits; GDI revisions; compensation excludes proprietors' income.

evidence.text: Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted 120,136 announced US job cuts citing artificial intelligence through September 2026, about 21% of all announced cuts and the leading reason so far this year, though AI was cited for about 9% of September's cuts (report of 1 October 2026). Total announced cuts of 573,195 were down 39% from the first nine months of 2025 (15% excluding government) and the lowest January-September total since 2022.
evidence.confounder: Announcements are not realized layoffs, and firms may name AI for investor messaging; the 2025 base was inflated by federal government cuts; technology accounts for 29% of 2026 cuts.

evidence.text: Commonwealth Bank of Australia reversed its July 2025 decision to cut 45 customer-service roles it planned to replace with an AI voice bot, after weeks of pressure from the Finance Sector Union and bank staff; a CBA spokesperson said the initial assessment did not adequately consider all relevant business considerations and the roles were not redundant (via Information Age, 21 August 2025).
evidence.via: a CBA spokesperson, via Information Age (corroborated by CNBC, which relays the ABC)
evidence.confounder: A single firm and small numbers; the reversal followed union pressure and a tribunal case, so it bears on backlash as much as on AI capability.

evidence.text: IBM's chief human resources officer Nickle LaMoreaux said in February 2026 that the company is tripling its entry-level hiring, including for software developers, with junior roles rewritten so that, for example, software engineers spend less time on routine coding and more with customers (via Fortune). CNBC reported the plan as tripling US entry-level hiring across all business units in 2026.
evidence.via: IBM CHRO Nickle LaMoreaux, via Fortune; also CNBC
evidence.confounder: A single firm; a stated plan with no numbers disclosed; IBM also moved HR work to AI.

evidence.text: The US city-average electricity price (fred:APU000072610) was $0.196 per kWh in August 2026, up 3.2% on a year earlier against 3.4% for the CPI (fred:CPIAUCSL), and the producer price index for power and distribution transformers (fred:WPU117409) rose 8.7% in the year to July 2026, the same as PPI all commodities (fred:PPIACO). Over longer spans both still outpaced the general indexes (electricity 15.3% against 9.2% over three years; transformers 86.6% against 39.2% from January 2021 to July 2026), so we read the past year as the premium pausing, not reversing.
evidence.confounder: The 2026 energy-price shock lifts the general indexes we compare against; regulated electricity rates adjust with a lag; the transformer PPI is a price proxy, not a lead-time measure; national averages hide data-center states.

nullCase.text: The Budget Lab at Yale, using August 2026 CPS data, finds no clear AI footprint in occupational change or in employment and unemployment by AI exposure, and prime-age employment, at 80.7% in September 2026, is above its January 2020 level. Atlanta Fed wage-growth gaps between professional and service occupations, and between finance and leisure industries, sit inside their 2015-2019 ranges, and in a Census survey only 2% of firms using AI reported employment reductions. New York Fed researchers find that the fall in postings for AI-exposed occupations began before ChatGPT.

gaps: 57 sources could not be opened (paywalls, or sites that block automated access); items rest on other copies or sources, and the list is in the run log.

We could not test whether the fall in labor-priced industries' share prices goes beyond their earnings changes: the Nasdaq industry indexes we use cover prices only, and this version of the tracker does not include the pinned stock basket with earnings.
We have no systematic measure of how share prices react to AI-linked job cuts. This edition rests on one company's reaction and one bank's study.

This edition has no evidence on seat and retention disclosures at the eight pinned per-seat software vendors, on revenue per employee against each pinned firm's pre-2022 trend, or on headcount at Wipro, HCLTech, Tech Mahindra, Concentrix, Teleperformance and the Philippine outsourcing industry.
This edition has no evidence from the law-school, bar-exam, nursing-exam, CPA or computing-degree data that the tracker lists as supply-side signals of where young people expect work.

No official data yet count new AI-era occupations (BLS occupation codes will not separate them before the 2028 revision), and no source measures new AI roles over time on the same basis as the losses.

No payment network or AI company has disclosed transaction volumes through agent payment rails, and this edition has no data on click-through when AI summaries appear or on how many pages AI crawlers take for each visit they send back.
This edition has no evidence on utilities' authorized returns, the top income decile's share of consumer spending, or how concentrated market value is among the largest US companies.
We cannot tell what share of liability policies carry the new generative-AI exclusions: the only count we found is 2,369 exclusion records in force across 49 states by mid-2026 (Insurance Business).
Third-quarter 2026 capex and results for the largest cloud companies are not yet reported, and Microsoft's is the only server depreciation-life assumption we have checked.
Our price series have no CPI item for legal services, so AI-exposed service prices rest on one mixed category and two specific items.
Registered apprenticeship figures for fiscal 2026 are incomplete until the last three months of the year are reported.
In this baseline, items dated before 2026 are marked as background.
